When Grandmother came to live with them, Arjun had to give up his room. It was the small room at the top of the stairs, with a window that looked over the mango tree. He had painted one wall blue himself, and he kept his cricket bat, his comics and a jar of marbles there. Now his father carried the bat and the comics down to the hall, and Grandmother's iron trunk went up in their place.

Arjun was given a mattress in the corner of his little sister's room. Meena was six. She talked in her sleep and woke up at five to sing. "It's only for a while," his mother said, but Arjun knew that Grandmother had come to stay. He was polite to her at dinner, and he answered her questions with one word. At night he lay on the mattress and listened to the mango leaves outside a window that was no longer his.

One afternoon, the power went off and the house became hot and still. Arjun climbed the stairs to fetch a book he had left behind, and found Grandmother sitting by his window with the jar of marbles in her lap. "I found these under the bed," she said. "When I was a girl in Thanjavur, I was the best marble player in our street. The boys were afraid of me."

Arjun did not believe her. She drew a circle on the floor with a piece of chalk from her trunk, and set the marbles inside it. Then she knelt, closed one eye and flicked. Three marbles shot out of the circle at once. Arjun stared. "Your turn," she said. They played until the power came back and the fan began to turn. He lost every game. When his mother called them for tea, Grandmother whispered, "Tomorrow I will teach you how to hold your thumb."

After that, Arjun went up to the room every afternoon. Grandmother taught him to hold his thumb, and in return he taught her to play cricket on the terrace with a tennis ball. She could not run, so she bowled, slowly and very straight. She told him stories about her village, and he told her about his school and about the boy who sat behind him and kicked his chair.

At the end of the term, Arjun's father asked whether he wanted his room back. "We could put Grandmother downstairs, in the hall," he said. Arjun thought about the narrow hall, with people walking through it all day. Then he thought about the window and the mango tree.

"No," he said. "She likes the window. And anyway, it is our room now." That evening he carried his cricket bat back up the stairs and leaned it against her trunk, where it belonged.

The old well at the end of Gandhi Street had been dry for years. People threw rubbish into it, and in the rains it filled with green water and mosquitoes. Children were told to keep away. Fatima walked past it every morning on her way to school and held her breath.

One day her teacher asked the class to find a problem in their own street and to think of a way to solve it. Most children wrote about broken street lights or noisy dogs. Fatima wrote about the well. "It could be useful again," she wrote, "if somebody cleaned it." Her teacher read the page and said, "Who is somebody?" Fatima did not have an answer. That evening she stood by the well with her friend Ravi and looked down into the smell.

Mr Pillai said the well had been dry since his father's time and nothing could be done. But Mrs D'Souza promised two buckets and a rope, and the tailor said he would come after he closed his shop.

On Sunday morning, eleven people arrived with gloves, buckets and sacks. They pulled out plastic bags, bottles, a broken chair and a bicycle wheel. By noon the smell was gone. A man from the water office, who had heard about it from his niece, came to look. He shone a torch down and said that the rains had not been reaching the well because the drain beside it was blocked. If the drain was cleared, he said, water might come back.

For the school science fair, Kavya wanted to answer a question that had bothered her for weeks: do plants grow better with music? Her uncle said that his tomatoes grew faster when the radio was on. Her brother said that was nonsense. Kavya decided to find out properly.

She took six small pots, filled each with the same soil, and planted three bean seeds in each. Three pots went in her bedroom, where she played music for two hours every evening. The other three went in the kitchen, where it was quiet. She gave every pot the same cup of water each morning and wrote everything in a notebook: the date, the time, and the height of every shoot, measured with a ruler. "A fair test," her teacher had said, "changes only one thing."

After two weeks, the bedroom beans were clearly taller. Kavya was delighted. She began to write a poster called Music Makes Plants Grow, and she told her uncle he had been right.

But when her teacher came to look, she asked a question Kavya had not thought of. "Is music the only difference between the bedroom and the kitchen?" Kavya thought. The bedroom window faced east and got the morning sun. The kitchen was darker, and it was warmer near the stove. "So the light was different too," her teacher said, "and the warmth. Your beans might be taller because of the sun, not the songs." Kavya looked at her poster and felt her face grow hot. Two weeks of work, and she could not say what it meant.

Kavya started again. This time she put all six pots on the same windowsill in the bedroom, side by side, so they had the same light and warmth. She placed a cardboard screen between them and played music only to the three on the left, using small earphones taped to the pots so the others would hear as little as possible.

After two more weeks, she measured again. The two groups were almost exactly the same height: on average, the music beans were half a centimetre taller, which was smaller than the difference between two beans in the same pot. She changed the title of her poster to Music Made No Clear Difference, and she added a box called What I Learned About Fair Tests.

At the fair, a judge spent a long time at her table. Kavya did not win first prize. But the judge wrote on her card: "Best change of mind in the hall."

Every year, between January and March, olive ridley turtles come ashore on the beach near Sanjay's village to lay their eggs. They come at night, in hundreds, and dig holes in the sand with their back flippers. Each turtle lays about a hundred eggs, covers them, and returns to the sea. She never sees her young.

When Sanjay was small, people took the eggs to eat or to sell, and dogs dug up the rest. Fewer turtles came each year. Then a group of fishermen, including Sanjay's father, started a hatchery: a fenced square of sand where eggs could be moved and kept safe. This year, for the first time, Sanjay was allowed to join the night patrol. He was twelve, and he had been waiting for this since he was eight.

The patrol walked the beach in the dark with red torches, because white light confuses the turtles. Sanjay's job was to watch for tracks: two lines of flipper marks with a groove between them, leading up from the water. Near midnight he found one. At the end of it, a turtle was digging, sand flying behind her.

They waited until she had finished laying and gone back to the sea. Then, very gently, Sanjay's father dug down and lifted the eggs out one by one. They were soft and white, like ping-pong balls. Sanjay counted them into a bucket of damp sand: one hundred and seven. In the hatchery they dug a new hole of the same depth and laid the eggs in it in the same order. Sanjay wrote the date and the number on a small wooden stick and pushed it into the sand.

Fifty days later, Sanjay was at the hatchery at dawn when the sand above his nest began to move. A tiny flipper appeared, then a head, then dozens of baby turtles, each no bigger than his palm, scrambling over each other. He counted ninety-one.

The hatchlings must reach the sea by themselves; the walk across the sand helps them remember the beach, so that the females can return to it one day to lay their own eggs. Sanjay walked beside them, chasing away a crow, until the last one was lifted by a wave and gone.

Only about one hatchling in a thousand lives to grow up. Sanjay knew that. But as he walked home, he thought about the female among his ninety-one who might, in fifteen years, crawl up this same beach on a dark night. He decided he would be there with a red torch to meet her.

The photograph appeared on Nikhil's phone during lunch: a crowd of people pushing at the gate of the town's water tank, and a caption in large red letters: WATER POISONED, DO NOT DRINK. SHARE NOW! It had come from his cousin, who had got it from a family group. By the time Nikhil looked up, three other people at his table had it too. Someone said the hospital was full. Someone else said his mother had already poured away all their water.

Nikhil's first thought was to send it to everyone he knew. His thumb was already on the button. Then he remembered something his grandfather, who had worked for a newspaper for forty years, always said: "A story that asks you to hurry is a story that does not want you to think." Nikhil put the phone down and looked at the picture again, more slowly.

Looked at slowly, the picture had problems. The people in it wore coats and woollen hats, although it was April and over thirty degrees in town. The sign above the gate was in a language Nikhil could not read. And the water tank in his town was blue, while this one was grey.

After school he showed it to his grandfather. The old man did not answer at once. He typed a few words into a search, then turned the screen towards Nikhil. The same photograph appeared in a news report from another country, four years earlier. The crowd had been waiting for a football match to open its gates. Nobody had poisoned anything.

"Then where did the caption come from?" Nikhil asked. "Someone added it," his grandfather said. "Maybe as a joke, maybe to frighten people. The picture is real. The story attached to it is not."

That evening Nikhil wrote a short message to his class group. He did not call anyone a liar. He put the photograph next to the old news report and wrote: "This picture is from another country, four years ago, at a football ground. Our tank is blue. The town council says the water is safe. Please check before you share." He added the link to the council's notice.

Some people thanked him. One boy said he was spoiling the fun. His cousin was quiet for a day and then posted the same message to the family group, where it was shared more times than the photograph had been.

The next week, Nikhil's teacher asked the class to bring in one news story and to answer three questions about it: Who made this? How do they know? What do they want me to do? Nikhil noticed that his own question had become the class's homework.

In 1924, a young clerk named Rangan saw a notice pinned to the wall of the post office in Madras. A race would be held on the beach road: ten miles, open to all. The winner would be sent to run in a national meeting in Bombay. Rangan had never raced, but he had walked eight miles to work and back every day for three years, and his legs were hard as wood.

He had no running shoes. On the morning of the race he ran barefoot, in a white vest his mother had sewn the night before. Most of the other runners were students from the colleges, in proper kit, with friends cheering. Nobody cheered for Rangan. At the halfway point he was twentieth. By the eighth mile he was fourth, and the students had stopped laughing.

Rangan finished second, eleven seconds behind a tall student called Edward. The prize to go to Bombay was Edward's. But the judge, an old Scottish teacher, came to find Rangan at the finish line. "You ran half the race too slowly," he said, "because you did not know you could win. Next year you will know."

For a year, Rangan trained before dawn on the beach, when the sand was cool. The teacher lent him a watch and showed him how to run each mile at the same speed instead of starting fast and slowing down. He found a pair of second-hand canvas shoes, and he learned that he preferred to run without them.

In 1925 he stood at the start of the beach-road race again. This time some of the clerks from the post office had come to watch. They had made a paper sign with his name on it.

Rangan won by a full minute. Two months later he ran in Bombay, against the best runners from every province, and came third. A newspaper printed his photograph under the words "Barefoot Clerk Surprises Bombay." The post office gave him a day's holiday.

He never ran in another country, and his name is not in the record books. He went back to his desk and worked at the post office for forty years. But every year until he was old, he walked to the beach road on race day and stood at the eighth mile, the place where he had once been fourth and had first understood that he might win. There, he cheered loudest for the runners nobody else was cheering for.

This story is told in Madras families, as stories are, and some of its details may have grown in the telling. The race, though, was real.

On the first day of term, a new boy called Tenzin sat alone at the end of the lunch bench. He had come from the hills, and his tiffin box smelled of something nobody in the class had eaten before. Two boys held their noses and laughed. Tenzin closed the box and ate nothing.

Priya saw it happen. She wanted to say something, but the boys were her friends, and she did not want them to laugh at her too. So she looked at her own lunch and said nothing. All afternoon she felt as if she had swallowed a stone. When the bell rang, Tenzin was the first out of the gate, walking fast with his head down.

The next day Priya did something brave, though it did not feel brave at the time. She carried her tiffin to the end of the bench and sat down next to Tenzin. "What is in your box?" she asked. He looked at her as if she might be joking. Then he opened it. Inside were small round dumplings. "Momos," he said. "My grandmother makes them."

Priya tried one. It was soft and warm, with vegetables inside and a spicy sauce. "These are better than my lunch," she said, and it was true. She gave him half of her lemon rice. The two boys watched from the other end of the bench, but this time they did not laugh.

By Friday, four children were sitting at the end of the bench, and Tenzin's grandmother was sending a bigger box. Even one of the boys who had laughed asked, a little shyly, if he could try a momo. Tenzin gave him two.

At the end of the month, the class held a food day, and everyone brought something from home. Tenzin's momos were finished first. Priya brought lemon rice, and she told the class about the first day, and how she had stayed quiet. "Next time," she said, "I will not wait until the next day." Tenzin smiled at her across the room. He no longer ate at the end of the bench. Now the bench had no end that anyone sat alone at.

questions.prompt: Whose food was finished first on food day?
questions.right: Tenzin's momos
wrong: Priya's lemon rice
The boys' sandwiches
questions.explain: Tenzin's momos were finished first.

questions.right: To speak up at once when someone is treated unkindly

To stop eating lunch with her old friends

whole.right: Standing up for someone who is left out

Winning a food competition

whole.right: From staying silent to acting kindly and speaking up

From shy at home to bold at school

parts.text:
Our school team needed eight runs from the last over to win the inter-school cricket final. Karthik, our best batsman, was out. The only batsmen left were Anil, who had scored nothing all season, and me. I was the team's scorer, and I had been sent in only because two players were ill.

My hands were shaking as I walked to the crease. The bowler from the other school was tall and fast, and his team was already clapping. Anil came up to me and said, "Just touch the ball and run. Don't try anything big." That was the best advice anyone gave me that day.

questions.prompt: How many runs did the team need from the last over?
questions.right: Eight
wrong: Six
Twelve
questions.explain: Our school team needed eight runs from the last over to win.

questions.prompt: Why was the narrator nervous?
questions.right: He was the scorer and not a real batsman
wrong: He had been ill the week before
The match was being played at night
questions.explain: He was the team's scorer, sent in only because two players were ill.

parts.text:
The first ball was so fast I did not see it. It thudded into the keeper's gloves. The second I pushed towards the edge of the field, and we ran two. The third I missed again. Then Anil said, "Watch his hand, not his face." On the fourth ball I did, and I saw the ball come out low and straight. I put my bat in front of it, and it ran away past the bowler. We ran three.

Three runs needed from two balls. On the fifth ball, Anil swung hard, and the ball flew high into the air. A fielder ran under it. Everyone went quiet. Then the ball slipped through his fingers and bounced away. We ran two.

questions.prompt: What did Anil tell the narrator to watch?
questions.right: The bowler's hand
wrong: The bowler's face
The fielders
questions.explain: "Watch his hand, not his face."

questions.prompt: What happened on the fifth ball?
questions.right: The ball was dropped and they ran two
wrong: The narrator was bowled out
Anil hit the ball for four runs
questions.explain: A fielder ran under it; the ball slipped through his fingers and they ran two.

parts.text:
One run to win, one ball to go. I was facing. The bowler ran in faster than ever. I watched his hand, as Anil had told me, and I did not swing. I just touched the ball and ran. Anil ran too, harder than I had ever seen anyone run, and he dived over the line as the ball hit the stumps behind him.

The umpire raised his finger slowly, and for a moment I thought Anil was out. Then I understood: he was signalling the run. We had won. The team ran onto the field and lifted Anil onto their shoulders. That evening, in the scorebook, I wrote my own name for the first time: Sameer, 6 not out. Next to Anil's name I wrote 2, and next to it, in small letters, "the best two runs of the season."

questions.prompt: How many runs did the narrator score?
questions.right: Six
wrong: Two
Eight
questions.explain: He wrote: Arjun, 6 not out.

questions.prompt: Why did Sameer call Anil's runs the best of the season?
questions.right: Anil's advice and running won the match
wrong: Anil hit the most sixes
Anil scored the first runs
questions.explain: Anil's advice and his dive over the line won the final.

whole.prompt: What is the main idea of the story?
whole.right: Calm teamwork can win when stars are missing
wrong: Fast bowlers always win in the end
Scorers should never be asked to bat
whole.explain: Two unlikely batsmen win by keeping calm and helping each other.

whole.prompt: How does Sameer change during the over?
whole.right: From shaking with fear to calm and focused
wrong: From calm and sure to frightened
From proud of himself to angry
whole.explain: His hands shook at first; by the last ball he watched the hand and did not swing.

whole.prompt: Why is the story called The Last Over?
whole.right: The whole story takes place in the final six balls
wrong: It is about the last match of the season
The bowler is called Over
whole.explain: The story follows each ball of the final over.

parts.text:
When Kavin's family moved to the city, his grandmother stayed behind in the village. She had a phone, but she used it only to answer calls, holding it far from her ear and shouting. Every Sunday Kavin's mother called her, and every Sunday the call ended with Grandmother saying, "I cannot see you. What use is a voice without a face?"

For his birthday, Kavin's uncle gave him some money. Kavin did not buy the cricket bat he had been wanting. Instead, he bought a second-hand smartphone and posted it to the village, with a note: "Grandmother, wait for Sunday."

questions.prompt: What did Grandmother complain about every Sunday?
questions.right: She could not see her family
wrong: The calls were too long
Her phone was broken
questions.explain: "I cannot see you. What use is a voice without a face?"

questions.prompt: What does Kavin's choice show about him?
questions.right: He cared more for his grandmother than a new bat
wrong: He did not really like playing cricket
He wanted a new phone for himself
questions.explain: He spent his birthday money on a phone for her instead of the bat he wanted.

parts.text:
Sunday did not go well. Grandmother answered the video call holding the phone to her ear, so the family saw only a grey plait of hair. When she finally looked at the screen, she pressed something, and the call ended. It took six attempts before her face appeared, upside down and very close.

Kavin realised that a phone alone was not enough. Every evening that week, he called her and taught her one small thing: how to hold the phone in front of her, which green button to press, how to turn the camera round. He drew pictures of the buttons on paper and asked the neighbour's daughter to stick them next to Grandmother's phone. Some evenings she was impatient. "In my day we wrote letters," she grumbled. But she always picked up.

questions.prompt: What did the family see first on the video call?
questions.right: A grey plait of hair
wrong: Grandmother's smiling face
A blank screen
questions.explain: She held the phone to her ear, so they saw only a grey plait of hair.

questions.prompt: Why did Kavin draw pictures of the buttons?
questions.right: To help her remember which to press
wrong: To decorate the walls of her house
For a project he had at school
questions.explain: He drew the buttons so she could follow them next to her phone.

parts.text:
On the next Sunday, the phone rang in the city. It was Grandmother, calling them. Her face filled the screen, the right way up, and behind her they could see her garden, where the beans were climbing the fence. She showed them a new calf, which tried to lick the phone, and the whole family laughed.

Now she calls on Wednesdays as well. She has learned to send photographs of her vegetables and to ask Kavin what he ate for lunch. Last month she showed her friend from the next street how to make a video call too. "It is not so difficult," she told her. "You only need a patient teacher." Kavin still has no new cricket bat. He says the calls are worth more.

questions.prompt: What did Grandmother show the family on the call?
questions.right: A new calf
wrong: A new house
Her new glasses
questions.explain: She showed them a new calf, which tried to lick the phone.

questions.prompt: What does "You only need a patient teacher" tell us?
questions.right: Kavin's patient teaching made the difference
wrong: Phones are able to teach themselves
Her friend works as a teacher
questions.explain: She credits patient teaching for her learning.

whole.prompt: What is the central theme of the story?
whole.right: Patience and care can bring a family closer
wrong: Old people should not use phones
Cricket bats cost too much money
whole.explain: Kavin's patient teaching lets Grandmother see her family again.

whole.prompt: How does Grandmother change?
whole.right: From giving up on phones to teaching a friend
wrong: From cheerful and calm to grumpy
From busy all day to bored at home
whole.explain: She could not answer a call at first, and later shows her friend how.

whole.prompt: What is shown by calling the story Grandmother's Video Call?
whole.right: The call is the goal everyone works towards
wrong: It is an advertisement for a phone
Grandmother invented video calls
whole.explain: The whole story builds to Grandmother making the call herself.

parts.text:
Every year before the harvest festival, our street held a kolam competition. Each family drew a pattern in rice flour on the ground outside their gate, and the oldest woman on the street walked along at sunrise to choose the best. For three years, the prize had gone to Mrs Lakshmi at number twelve, whose kolams were so large and perfect that people from other streets came to photograph them.

This year my sister Anitha, who was eleven, announced that she would win. Our mother laughed and said it was enough to take part. Anitha did not laugh. For two weeks she practised in a notebook every evening, drawing dots and curves until her pencil was a stub.

questions.prompt: What were the kolams drawn with?
questions.right: Rice flour
wrong: Coloured chalk
Paint
questions.explain: Each family drew a pattern in rice flour on the ground.

questions.prompt: What does practising every evening show about Anitha?
questions.right: She was determined
wrong: She was bored
She disliked drawing
questions.explain: She practised for two weeks until her pencil was a stub.

parts.text:
On the night before the festival, Anitha got up at four. She swept the ground, sprinkled water to settle the dust, and began. Her design was not large. It was a peacock, made of a single unbroken line that looped around a grid of dots, so that you could follow it with your finger from beak to tail and back again without lifting it.

At five, it started to drizzle. Anitha covered half the kolam with our umbrella and stood in the rain over the other half, holding a plastic sheet. By the time the rain stopped, she was soaked, but only one feather had smudged. She redrew it carefully as the sky turned pink.

questions.prompt: What was special about Anitha's peacock?
questions.right: It was one unbroken line
wrong: It was the largest on the street
It used many colours
questions.explain: It was made of a single unbroken line that looped around a grid of dots.

questions.prompt: Why was Anitha soaked?
questions.right: She protected her kolam from the rain
wrong: She fell into a puddle on the way
She had washed the whole street
questions.explain: She stood in the rain holding a plastic sheet over the kolam.

parts.text:
At sunrise, old Mrs Rangan walked slowly along the street with her stick. She stopped for a long time at number twelve, where Mrs Lakshmi's kolam covered the whole road like a carpet. Then she came to our gate. She bent down, put her finger on the peacock's beak, and traced the line all the way round. It took her a full minute.

She gave the prize to Mrs Lakshmi. Anitha's face fell. But then Mrs Rangan turned to her and said, "Yours is the one I will remember. A line that never breaks is the hardest thing to draw." That afternoon, Mrs Lakshmi came to our house with a plate of sweets and asked Anitha to teach her the peacock. Next year, she said, they would draw one together.

questions.prompt: Who won the prize?
questions.right: Mrs Lakshmi
wrong: Anitha
Mrs Rangan
questions.explain: She gave the prize to Mrs Lakshmi.

questions.prompt: Why did Mrs Lakshmi visit with sweets?
questions.right: She admired Anitha's skill and wanted to learn
wrong: She wanted to show off her prize
She was a relative visiting
questions.explain: She asked Anitha to teach her the peacock.

whole.prompt: What is the central theme of the story?
whole.right: Skill and care can earn respect even without winning
wrong: Big kolams always win the prize in the end
Rain always spoils a festival morning
whole.explain: Anitha does not win, but her skill earns the judge's and the winner's respect.

whole.prompt: How do Anitha's feelings change at the end?
whole.right: From disappointed to proud and welcomed
wrong: From happy at first to angry
From bored and tired to sleepy
whole.explain: Her face fell at losing, then the judge and Mrs Lakshmi honoured her work.

whole.prompt: Why is the story called The Kolam Competition rather than Anitha's Win?
whole.right: Because she does not win, yet gains something better
wrong: Because Anitha won the prize
Because kolams are not drawn at festivals
whole.explain: The competition is the setting; the real reward is respect and friendship.

parts.text:
The trek to the waterfall had been planned for months, and by eight in the morning our group of six was already high on the forest path, with the guide, Mr Joseph, walking in front. The air smelled of wet leaves and cardamom. Below us, the valley lay like a green bowl, and the river shone in the sun.

By ten, everything had changed. A white fog rolled up the hillside so quickly that within minutes we could not see the person walking in front of us. Mr Joseph stopped and made us hold hands in a line. "Nobody leaves the path," he said quietly. "In fog, the forest looks the same in every direction."

questions.prompt: Why did Mr Joseph make the group hold hands?
questions.right: Fog made it impossible to see each other
wrong: The path was slippery with mud
A wild animal was near
questions.explain: In the fog they could not see the person walking in front of them.

questions.prompt: What does "the forest looks the same in every direction" warn about?
questions.right: It is easy to get lost
wrong: The forest is boring
The trees are all the same kind
questions.explain: In fog, without landmarks, walkers easily lose their way.

parts.text:
We walked slowly for an hour, listening to Mr Joseph's voice. Then my cousin Rohan, at the back of the line, let go to tie his lace. When he stood up, the line had moved on, and the fog had closed behind it. He called out, but the wet trees swallowed the sound.

Rohan remembered what Mr Joseph had told us at the start, though most of us had not been listening: if you are lost, stay where you are, make yourself warm, and make a noise that carries. He sat under a large rock, put on his rain jacket, and blew the whistle every member of the group had been given, three short blasts, again and again.

questions.prompt: Why was Rohan separated from the group?
questions.right: He let go to tie his lace
wrong: He chased a bird
He fell into the river
questions.explain: He let go to tie his lace, and the line moved on.

questions.prompt: What signal did Rohan make with his whistle?
questions.right: Three short blasts, again and again
wrong: One long blast every hour
A song he had learnt at school
questions.explain: He blew three short blasts, again and again.

parts.text:
It was Mr Joseph who noticed first that the line was one person short. He did not let anyone go back alone. Instead, he tied a rope from the last person to a tree and walked back along the path, counting his steps and stopping every fifty to listen. On the third stop, he heard it: three short blasts, faint but clear, to the left of the path.

Rohan was found shivering but smiling. The fog lifted an hour later, and we saw that he had sat only forty metres from the path, beside a drop of twenty metres that he had never seen. Nobody felt like reaching the waterfall that day. On the walk down, Mr Joseph said that the forest had taught us more than any waterfall could: that the rules we half-listen to at the start are the ones that bring us home.

questions.prompt: How did Mr Joseph keep himself from getting lost while searching?
questions.right: A rope tied to a tree and counting his steps
wrong: He used a map and compass
He followed Rohan's footprints
questions.explain: He tied a rope to a tree and counted his steps, stopping to listen.

questions.prompt: Why was it lucky that Rohan stayed where he was?
questions.right: A dangerous drop was right beside him
wrong: He was close to the waterfall
Staying kept him dry
questions.explain: He had sat beside a twenty-metre drop he had never seen.

whole.prompt: What is the central theme of the story?
whole.right: Safety rules matter most when things go wrong
wrong: Waterfalls are not worth the walk
Fog in the hills is beautiful
whole.explain: Following the rules he half-heard brought Rohan home safely.

whole.prompt: What does Mr Joseph's search show about him?
whole.right: He is calm and careful in a crisis
wrong: He is careless and in a hurry
He is frightened and gives up
whole.explain: He searched methodically with a rope and counting, not in a panic.

whole.prompt: Why is the story called Fog on the Western Ghats?
whole.right: The fog causes the danger at the heart of the story
wrong: It is a weather report for the hills
The group went there to study the fog
whole.explain: The sudden fog separates Rohan and creates the danger.

texts.title: The Mystery of the Missing Sugar

parts.text:
Somebody was stealing sugar from the kitchen. Every morning, Divya's mother found the lid of the sugar tin slightly open and a thin white trail across the counter. Divya's younger brother Varun was the first to be suspected, because he had once been caught eating sugar with a spoon. He swore he had not touched it, and for once Divya believed him.

Divya decided to investigate as a scientist would. "First we observe," she said, "then we guess, then we test the guess." She did not accuse anyone. That night, she sprinkled a little flour on the counter around the tin, so that anything that walked there would leave tracks.

questions.prompt: What clue did Divya's mother find each morning?
questions.right: A thin white trail and an open lid
wrong: Footprints on the floor
An empty tin
questions.explain: She found the lid slightly open and a thin white trail across the counter.

questions.prompt: Why did Divya sprinkle flour around the tin?
questions.right: To catch the tracks of whatever came
wrong: To bake a cake for her brother
To hide the sugar from the thief
questions.explain: Anything walking there would leave tracks in the flour.

parts.text:
In the morning, there were no footprints, not even small ones. Instead, the flour was crossed by hundreds of tiny dotted lines, all leading from a crack beside the window to the sugar tin and back. Divya looked closely with her father's magnifying glass and saw them: a moving line of very small ants, each carrying a grain of sugar almost as big as its own head.

Varun was delighted to be innocent. But Divya was not finished. "Our guess is ants," she said. "Now we test it. If ants are the thieves, then sugar in a tin with a tight lid should stay safe, and a little sugar left outside should disappear." She placed a teaspoon of sugar on a saucer and closed the tin firmly.

questions.prompt: Where did the ant trails lead from?
questions.right: A crack beside the window
wrong: The kitchen door
Under the fridge
questions.explain: The lines led from a crack beside the window to the sugar tin.

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of the saucer of sugar?
questions.right: To test whether ants were the thieves
wrong: To give Varun a sweet treat
To catch the mice in the kitchen
questions.explain: If ants were the thieves, sugar left outside should disappear.

parts.text:
By evening, the saucer was empty and the tin was untouched. The guess had passed its test. Divya's father wanted to spray the crack with poison, but Divya asked him to wait. She had read that ants follow a scent trail left by the ants before them. She wiped the counter with vinegar to remove the trail, sealed the crack with a little putty, and kept the sugar in a jar with a screw lid.

The ants did not come back. At dinner, her mother announced that the case was closed, and Varun asked for an apology, which he received, along with a small spoon of sugar. Divya wrote up the case in her science notebook under the heading "Observe, guess, test" and added a fourth word underneath: "Explain."

questions.prompt: Why did Divya wipe the counter with vinegar?
questions.right: To remove the ants' scent trail
wrong: To clean up spilt sugar
To make the kitchen smell nice
questions.explain: Ants follow a scent trail, so she removed it with vinegar.

questions.prompt: Why did Divya add the word "Explain"?
questions.right: A scientist also says why the answer is right
wrong: She forgot to explain to Varun
Her teacher told her to
questions.explain: Testing gives an answer; explaining shows why it works.

whole.prompt: What is the central theme of the story?
whole.right: Careful observing and testing finds the truth
wrong: Younger brothers always steal sugar
Ants are dangerous pests at home
whole.explain: Divya solves the mystery by observing, guessing and testing, not by blaming.

whole.prompt: How does Divya behave differently from the rest of her family?
whole.right: She tests ideas instead of accusing or spraying
wrong: She blames her brother Varun first
She ignores the problem completely
whole.explain: Others suspected Varun or wanted poison; she observed and tested.

whole.prompt: Why is the story called a mystery?
whole.right: The thief is unknown until it is investigated
wrong: Because nobody ever finds the thief
Because the sugar was magic
whole.explain: The family does not know who is taking the sugar until Divya's test.
